pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A body when projected at an angle ' $\theta$ ' with the horizontal reaches a maximum height ' $H$ '. The time of flight of the body will be ( $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity)</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Relation for maximum height</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a projectile, the vertical component of velocity:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ u_y = u \sin\theta $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Maximum height:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ H = \frac{u_y^2}{2g} = \frac{(u \sin\theta)^2}{2g} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \therefore u \sin\theta = \sqrt{2gH} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Total time of flight</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Time of flight:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T = \frac{2 u \sin\theta}{g} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute $u \sin\theta = \sqrt{2gH}$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T = \frac{2 \sqrt{2gH}}{g} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ T = 2 \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{2 \sqrt{\tfrac{2H}{g}}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: C</prep-strong></prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Motion in Two Dimensions - Motion in a Plane

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Which of the following person is in an inertial frame of reference?</prep-p>

pyqs.b: A child revolving in a merry-go-round.
pyqs.c: A driver in a bus which is moving with constant velocity.
pyqs.d: A man in a train which is slowing down to stop.
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Option C: A driver in a bus which is moving with constant velocity.</prep-p>
<prep-p>An inertial frame of reference is defined as a frame where a body not subjected to external forces moves at a constant velocity, which includes being at rest. In this scenario, the bus moving with constant velocity implies that it is not accelerating, thereby making the driver in this bus an observer in an inertial frame of reference. </prep-p>
<prep-p>In contrast:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>Option A (aeroplane taking off) involves acceleration, hence it is a non-inertial frame.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Option B (child in a merry-go-round) experiences centripetal acceleration, making it a non-inertial frame.</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Option D (train slowing down) involves deceleration, thus it is not an inertial frame.</prep-p></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The power $(\mathrm{P})$ is supplied to a rotating body having moment of inertia ' I ' and angular acceleration ' $\alpha$ '. Its instantaneous angular velocity ' $\omega$ ' is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { Power }=\frac{\text { Work done }}{\text { time }} \\
& \mathrm{P}=\frac{\text { Torque } \times \text { angular displacement }}{\text { time }}=\tau \times \omega
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\ldots\left[\because \omega=\frac{\theta}{t}\right] \quad \ldots(\because \tau=I \alpha)$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore\quad\mathrm{P} & =\mathrm{I} \alpha \omega \\
\therefore\quad\omega & =\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{I} \alpha} \\
& =\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{I} \alpha)^{-1}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The total energy of a circularly orbiting satellite is</prep-p>
pyqs.a: half the kinetic energy of the satellite.
pyqs.b: half the potential energy of the satellite.
pyqs.c: twice the kinetic energy of the satellite.
pyqs.d: twice the potential energy of the satellite.
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>First, recall the NCERT results for a satellite of mass $m$ orbiting a planet of mass $M$ at radius $r$:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Gravitational potential energy:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$   U = -\frac{GMm}{r}   $$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Kinetic energy:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$   K = \frac{GMm}{2r}   $$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>The total energy $E$ is the sum of kinetic and potential energy:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E = K + U $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute the values:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E = \frac{GMm}{2r} + \left(-\frac{GMm}{r}\right) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E = \frac{GMm}{2r} - \frac{GMm}{r} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E = -\frac{GMm}{2r} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now compare $E$ with $K$ and $U$:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$E = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = -K$</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$U = -\frac{GMm}{r} = 2E$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>Therefore, the total energy is <prep-strong>half the potential energy</prep-strong> of the satellite.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: half the potential energy of the satellite.</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>At what speed should a source of sound move so that the observer finds the apparent frequency equal to half the original frequency?</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1. Recall Doppler effect formula</prep-h3>
<prep-p>When the <prep-strong>source</prep-strong> is moving (with constant velocity) and the observer is stationary, the apparent frequency $ f' $ is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ f' = f \cdot \frac{v}{v + v_s} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ f $ = actual frequency,  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ v $ = speed of sound in air,  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ v_s $ = speed of source (positive if source is moving <prep-strong>away</prep-strong> from observer).</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 2. Condition given</prep-h3>
<prep-p>We want the apparent frequency to be <prep-strong>half</prep-strong> the original:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ f' = \frac{f}{2} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute in the formula:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{f}{2} = f \cdot \frac{v}{v + v_s} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Cancel $ f $:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{1}{2} = \frac{v}{v + v_s} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3. Solve for $ v_s $</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Cross multiply:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v + v_s = 2v $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ v_s = v $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4. Final Answer</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The source should move with speed equal to the speed of sound $ V $.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option: D (V).</prep-strong> ✅</prep-p>

<prep-p>The formula for the time period is given as $$
\mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{\mathrm{~g}}}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The mass of displaced fluid is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \text { Mass }=\text { density } \times \text { volume } \\
& \mathrm{m}=\rho \times \mathrm{A} l
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>At equilibrium,</prep-p>
<prep-p>Weight of the block $$=$$ Weight of the displaced liquid</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{mg}=\mathrm{A} l \rho \mathrm{g} \\
& \therefore \quad l=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{A} \rho}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substituting the values in the equation</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{l}{\mathrm{~g}}} \\
& \mathrm{~T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{Apg}}}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The frequency $$f=\frac{1}{T}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\therefore \quad \mathrm{f}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{Apg}}{\mathrm{m}}}$$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A conducting sphere of radius ' R ' is given a charge ' $Q$ ' uniformly. The electric field and the electric potential at the centre of the sphere are respectively [ $\varepsilon_0=$ permittivity of free space]</prep-p>

<prep-h3>1. Electric Field at the Centre of a Conducting Sphere</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a <prep-strong>conducting sphere</prep-strong>, the <prep-strong>electric field inside</prep-strong> (including at the centre) is <prep-strong>zero</prep-strong>. This is because charges reside only on the surface and inside the conductor the electric field is always zero (as per electrostatics in conductors).</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ E_{\text{centre}} = 0 $$</prep-p>

<prep-h3>2. Electric Potential at the Centre</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The <prep-strong>electric potential</prep-strong> at any point <prep-strong>inside</prep-strong> a uniformly charged conducting sphere (including its centre) is <prep-strong>equal to the potential at the surface</prep-strong>.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Potential at the surface is given by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ V = \frac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>This same value is also at the centre.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>3. Final Answer</prep-h3>
<prep-p>So, <prep-strong>electric field at the centre = 0</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Potential at the centre = $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 R}$</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-h3>4. Option Matching</prep-h3>
<prep-p>This matches with <prep-strong>Option A</prep-strong>.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A:</prep-strong> zero and $\frac{Q}{4\pi \varepsilon_0 R}$</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Substitute given errors</prep-h3>

</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So:  </prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>A point mass ' $m$ ' attached at one end of a massless, inextensible string of length ' $l$ ' performs a vertical circular motion and the string rotates in vertical plane, as shown in the diagram. The increase in the centripetal acceleration of the point mass when it moves from point A to point C is</prep-p>
<prep-p>[ $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity.]</prep-p><prep-img src="https://mkvdpokqofzstcoifhzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/pyq-images/Physics/2614.jpg" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-height: 40vh; vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2025 25th April Morning Shift Physics - Circular Motion Question 4 English">
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-img src="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/fly/@width/image/jaoe38c1mf5w677l/94db99f4-1564-4166-890e-9a5c29433aa6/62164710-89d2-11f0-b077-f3e94c65b3e9/file-jaoe38c1mf5w677m.png?format=png" data-orsrc="https://app-content.cdn.examgoal.net/image/jaoe38c1mf5w677l/94db99f4-1564-4166-890e-9a5c29433aa6/62164710-89d2-11f0-b077-f3e94c65b3e9/file-jaoe38c1mf5w677m.png" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-height: 40vh; vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2025 25th April Morning Shift Physics - Circular Motion Question 4 English Explanation"><prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\text { By Conservation of energy, }\\ &\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{KE}_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathrm{PE}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{KE}_{\mathrm{C}}+\mathrm{PE}_{\mathrm{C}} \\ \therefore \quad & 2 \mathrm{mgl}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{c}}^2+\mathrm{mgl} \quad \ldots\left(\because \mathrm{At} \mathrm{~A}, \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}=0\right) \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \therefore \quad \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{C}}^2=2 \mathrm{gl} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>We know,</prep-p>
<prep-p>Centripetal acceleration $=\frac{\mathrm{v}^2}{\mathrm{r}}$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\ldots(\mathrm{r}=$ radius of circular motion $)$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ At point A ,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ a_A=\frac{v_A^2}{l} \Rightarrow a_A=0 \ldots\left(\because v_A=0\right) $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ At point C ,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{C}}^2}{\mathrm{l}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{C}}=2 \mathrm{~g} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ Increase in the centripetal acceleration of the point mass from point A to point C is 2 g</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The liquid (mercury) meniscus in capillary tube will be convex if the angle of contact is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Key Concept:</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>The <prep-strong>angle of contact</prep-strong> (or contact angle) is the angle between the tangent to the liquid surface at the point of contact and the solid surface <prep-strong>inside the liquid</prep-strong>.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>If the angle of contact <prep-strong>θ < 90°</prep-strong>, the liquid wets the surface → concave meniscus (e.g., water in glass tube).</prep-p></prep-li>

<prep-li><prep-p>If θ = 0°, perfect wetting → completely concave upward.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>If θ = 90°, theoretically flat at surface.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>For <prep-strong>mercury in glass</prep-strong>, the contact angle is around 128°, which is > 90°, hence the meniscus is <prep-strong>convex</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Option A: greater than $90^{\circ}$</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A black body has maximum wavelength ' $\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$ ' at temperature 2000 K . Its maximum wavelength at 3000 K will be</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We are dealing with <prep-strong>Wien’s displacement law</prep-strong>:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \lambda_m T = \text{constant} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>At temperature $T_1 = 2000\ \mathrm{K}$, the maximum wavelength is $\lambda_m$.  </prep-p>

<prep-p>Using Wien’s law:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \lambda_m T_1 = \lambda_m' T_2 $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \lambda_m' = \lambda_m \cdot \frac{T_1}{T_2} $</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>An ideal gas taken through a process ABCA as shown in figure. If the net heat supplied to gas in the cycle is 5 J , then the work done by the gas in process from C to A is</prep-p><prep-img src="https://mkvdpokqofzstcoifhzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/pyq-images/Physics/3014.jpg" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-height: 40vh; vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2025 26th April Evening Shift Physics - Heat and Thermodynamics Question 1 English">

<prep-p>Two cylinders A and B fitted with piston contain equal amount of an ideal diatomic gas at temperature T K. The piston of cylinder A is free to move while that of cylinder $B$ is held fixed. The same amount of heat is given to the gas in each cylinder. If the rise of temperature of the gas in A is $\mathrm{dT}_{\mathrm{A}}$, then the rise in temperature of the gas in B is $\left(\gamma=\frac{C_p}{C_v}\right)$</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall specific heats for diatomic ideal gas</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a diatomic gas (ignoring vibrational d.o.f. at moderate temperatures):</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ C_v = \frac{5}{2} R,  \quad C_p = C_v + R = \frac{7}{2} R $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \gamma = \frac{C_p}{C_v} = \frac{7/2}{5/2} = \frac{7}{5} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Heat supplied in each case</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>For cylinder A (isobaric):</prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$ Q = n C_p dT_A $</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li>For cylinder B (isochoric) with temperature rise $dT_B$:</prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>$ Q = n C_v dT_B $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since $Q$ is the same in both cases:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ n C_p dT_A = n C_v dT_B $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Relating temperature rises</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ dT_B = \frac{C_p}{C_v} dT_A = \gamma \, dT_A $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The rise in temperature of the gas in B is  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\gamma \, dT_A} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: C</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: A black body emits radiation of maximum intensity at wavelength ' $\lambda$ ' at temperature T K. Its corresponding wavelength at temperature 1.5 T K will be
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall Wien’s displacement law</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \lambda_{\text{max}} T = \text{constant} \quad (b) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \lambda_{\text{max}} \propto \frac{1}{T}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Compare two states</prep-h3>
<prep-p>At temperature $ T $,  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \lambda = \frac{b}{T}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>At temperature $ 1.5T $, the new wavelength is</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \lambda' = \frac{b}{1.5T}. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Relating $\lambda'$ and $\lambda$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \lambda' = \frac{b}{1.5T} = \frac{1}{1.5}\cdot \frac{b}{T} = \frac{1}{1.5}\cdot \lambda = \frac{\lambda}{1.5} = \frac{2}{3}\lambda. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \boxed{\tfrac{2 \lambda}{3}} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct Option: A</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The two ends of a rod of length ' $x$ ' and uniform cross-sectional area ' A ' are kept at temperatures ' $\mathrm{T}_1$ ' and ' $\mathrm{T}_2$ ' respectively ( $\mathrm{T}_1>\mathrm{T}_2$ ). If the rate of heat transfer is ' $\mathrm{Q} / \mathrm{t}$ ', through the rod in steady state, then the coefficient of thermal conductivity ' K ' is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We are asked about heat conduction through a rod.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>The formula for the rate of heat conduction is Fourier’s law:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{Q}{t} \;=\; \frac{K A (T_1 - T_2)}{x} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Where  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$K$ = thermal conductivity  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$A$ = cross-sectional area  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$x$ = length of the rod  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$(T_1 - T_2)$ = temperature difference  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\frac{Q}{t}$ = rate of heat flow  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p>Now we rearrange for $K$:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K = \frac{\tfrac{Q}{t} \cdot x}{A (T_1 - T_2)} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ K = \frac{x Q}{t A (T_1 - T_2)} $</prep-p>

<prep-p>✅ Correct option is:</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B:</prep-strong>  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{x Q}{t A \,(T_1 - T_2)} $</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>At certain temperature, $\operatorname{rod} \mathrm{A}$ and $\operatorname{rod} \mathrm{B}$ of different materials have lengths $\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\mathrm{L}_B$ respectively. Their co-efficients of linear expansion are $\alpha_A$ and $\alpha_B$ respectively. It is observed that the difference between their lengths remain constant at all temperatures. The ratio $L_A / L_B$ is given by</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let's analyze the problem step by step:</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-p>Assume that at some initial temperature, rod A has length $$L_A$$ and rod B has length $$L_B$$. When the temperature increases by $$\Delta T$$, the new lengths become:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\text{Rod A: } L_A(1 + \alpha_A \Delta T)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\text{Rod B: } L_B(1 + \alpha_B \Delta T)$$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>The condition given is that the difference between the lengths remains constant at all temperatures. This means:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$L_B(1 + \alpha_B \Delta T) - L_A(1 + \alpha_A \Delta T) = L_B - L_A$$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Expanding the left-hand side:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$L_B + L_B\alpha_B\Delta T - L_A - L_A\alpha_A\Delta T = L_B - L_A$$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Notice that the terms $$L_B$$ and $$-L_A$$ on both sides cancel, leaving:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$L_B\alpha_B\Delta T - L_A\alpha_A\Delta T = 0$$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Since $$\Delta T \neq 0$$, we can divide both sides by $$\Delta T$$ to obtain:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$L_B\alpha_B - L_A\alpha_A = 0$$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Rearranging the equation gives:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$L_A\alpha_A = L_B\alpha_B$$</prep-p></prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-p>Finally, dividing both sides by $$L_B\alpha_A$$ yields:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{L_A}{L_B} = \frac{\alpha_B}{\alpha_A}$$</prep-p></prep-p>

<prep-p>Thus, the required ratio is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{L_A}{L_B} = \frac{\alpha_B}{\alpha_A}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>This corresponds to Option B.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A particle is performing S.H.M. starting from extreme position. Graphical representation shows that between displacement and acceleration, there is a phase difference of</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall the SHM relations</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a particle in SHM,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \phi) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$x(t)$ = displacement</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$A$ = amplitude</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\omega$ = angular frequency</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\phi$ = phase constant</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>The acceleration is related to displacement by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ a(t) = \ddot{x}(t) = -\omega^2 x(t) $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Relationship between $x(t)$ and $a(t)$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>From the expression:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ a(t) = -\omega^2 x(t) $</prep-p>
<prep-p>This shows that <prep-strong>acceleration is directly proportional to displacement, but opposite in direction.</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Phase difference</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Both $a(t)$ and $x(t)$ vary sinusoidally with the <prep-strong>same frequency</prep-strong>.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>However, $a(t)$ has a <prep-strong>negative sign</prep-strong> compared to displacement.</prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>This corresponds to a <prep-strong>phase difference of $\pi$ radians (180°).</prep-strong></prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-p>✅ <prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{Phase difference} = \pi \,\text{rad} $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: A. $\pi \, \text{rad}$</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Resolving power of a telescope can be increased by increasing</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The resolving power $ R $ of a telescope depends mainly on the <prep-strong>objective lens/mirror</prep-strong> and is given (approximately) by the Rayleigh criterion:</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Graph shows the variation of fringe width ( X ) versus distance of the screen from the plane of the slits (D) in Young's double slit experiment. (keeping other parameters same, $d=$ distance between the slits). The wavelength of light used can be calculated as</prep-p><prep-img src="https://mkvdpokqofzstcoifhzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/pyq-images/Physics/3489.jpg" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-height: 40vh; vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2025 26th April Evening Shift Physics - Wave Optics Question 1 English">
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The formula for fringe width in Young's double slit experiment is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$X = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Here, $X$ is the fringe width, $\lambda$ is the wavelength, $D$ is the distance from the slits to the screen, and $d$ is the distance between the two slits.</prep-p>
<prep-p>The graph shows how $X$ (fringe width) changes with $D$ (distance to the screen). This means the slope of the graph is $\frac{X}{D}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>From the formula above, if we write it as $\frac{X}{D} = \frac{\lambda}{d}$, we see that the slope of the graph equals $\frac{\lambda}{d}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, you can calculate $\lambda$ (wavelength) using:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\lambda = \text{slope} \times d$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Here, ‘slope’ means the value you get from the graph ($\frac{X}{D}$), and $d$ is the distance between the slits.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Kirchhoff's voltage law and current law are based (respectively) on the conservation of</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>We need to analyze:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL):</prep-strong> It states that the algebraic sum of currents entering a node is zero. This is directly based on the <prep-strong>conservation of electric charge</prep-strong>.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL):</prep-strong> It states that the algebraic sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero. This follows from the fact that energy is conserved — as a charge moves around a closed loop, the net energy gained and lost must equal zero.  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So:  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>KVL → <prep-strong>conservation of energy</prep-strong>  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>KCL → <prep-strong>conservation of charge</prep-strong></prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>✅ Correct answer is:  </prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Option B: energy, charge</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.explanation_content:

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Lorentz magnetic force is acting on a particle of charge q moving with velocity $\vec{V}$ in a magnetic field $\vec{B}$. The work done by this force on the charged particle is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The Lorentz force due to a magnetic field only is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \vec{F} = q \, \vec{V} \times \vec{B}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Now, the work done by a force in moving a particle is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{dW}{dt} = \vec{F} \cdot \vec{V}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \vec{F} \cdot \vec{V} = (q \, \vec{V} \times \vec{B}) \cdot \vec{V}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>But $\vec{V} \times \vec{B}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{V}$, so the dot product is zero.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Hence,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \frac{dW}{dt} = 0 \quad \implies \quad W = 0. $</prep-p>

<prep-p>✅ <prep-strong>Correct Answer: Option A (zero).</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>Two wires of equal lengths are bent in the form of a square and a circular loop. They are suspended in a uniform magnetic field and same current is passed through them. Torque experienced by</prep-p>
pyqs.b: <prep-p>both the loops is same but not zero.</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The formula for torque is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>

$$ \tau = IAB \sin \theta $$

where $\tau$ is torque, $I$ is current, $A$ is the area of the loop, $B$ is the magnetic field, and $\theta$ is the angle between the field and the normal to the loop.

</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since the current, magnetic field, and angle are the same for both shapes, the torque mainly depends on the area $A$ of each loop.</prep-p>
<prep-p>For a given length of wire (same perimeter), a circle always has a bigger area than a square.</prep-p>
<prep-p>So, the circular loop will experience a greater torque than the square loop.</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Torque on a Current Loop in Magnetic Field

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The magnetic field (B) inside a long solenoid having ' $n$ ' turns per unit length and carrying current ' i ' when iron core is kept in it, is ( $\mu_0=$ permeability of vacuum, $\chi=$ magnetic susceptibility)</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall field in a solenoid without core</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a long solenoid (no core, just vacuum/air inside), the field is:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ B_0 = \mu_0 n i $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ \mu_0 $ is permeability of free space,  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ n $ is number of turns per unit length,  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ i $ is the current.  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Include effect of core material</prep-h3>
<prep-p>If a core with magnetic susceptibility $ \chi $ is introduced, the relative permeability is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mu_r = 1 + \chi $</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the effective permeability is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mu = \mu_0 (1 + \chi) $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Final expression</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Now, the magnetic field becomes:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ B = \mu n i = \mu_0 (1 + \chi) n i $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4: Match with options</prep-h3>
<prep-p>That matches <prep-strong>Option A</prep-strong>:  </prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mu_0 \, n i (1 + \chi) $</prep-p>

<prep-p>✅ <prep-strong>Correct Answer: Option A</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: A long rectangular conducting loop of width ' $l$ ', mass ' $m$ ' and resistance ' $R$ ' is placed partly in a perpendicular magnetic field ' B '. It is pushed downwards with velocity ' $V$ ' so that it may continue to fall freely. The velocity ' $V$ ' is<prep-img src="https://mkvdpokqofzstcoifhzy.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/pyq-images/Physics/4082.jpg" loading="lazy" style="max-width: 100%; height: auto; display: block; margin: 0 auto; max-height: 40vh; vertical-align: baseline" alt="MHT CET 2025 26th April Evening Shift Physics - Electromagnetic Induction Question 2 English">
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 1: Find the induced emf</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>When the loop moves in the magnetic field, an emf (electric force) is created. The formula is: $$ E = l v B $$ where $l$ is the width of the loop, $v$ is the velocity, and $B$ is the magnetic field.</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 2: Find the induced current</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>According to Ohm's Law, $E = iR$, where $i$ is the current and $R$ is the resistance. So, $$ i = \frac{l v B}{R} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 3: Equate forces for free fall</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>If the loop is falling freely, the downward force (gravity) must equal the upward magnetic force. So, $$ mg = F_m $$ where $m$ is mass and $g$ is gravity.</prep-p>
<prep-p>The magnetic force ($F_m$) is given by $i l B$. So, $$ mg = i l B $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 4: Substitute the current value</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Substitute $i$ from step 2 into the force equation: $$ mg = \left(\frac{l v B}{R}\right) l B $$ $$ mg = \frac{l^2 v B^2}{R} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-b>Step 5: Solve for velocity $v$</prep-b></prep-p>
<prep-p>Rearrange for $v$: $$ v = \frac{mgR}{B^2 l^2} $$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>In an a.c. circuit containing $L, C, R$ in series the ratio of true power to apparent power is ( $\mathrm{Z}=$ impedance of the circuit and R is the resistance)</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1: Recall key concepts</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>True power (P)</prep-strong> = $ V I \cos \phi$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Apparent power (S)</prep-strong> = $ V I$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p><prep-strong>Power factor (p.f.)</prep-strong> = $ \dfrac{P}{S} = \cos \phi$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So, the ratio of true power to apparent power is <prep-strong>$\cos \phi$</prep-strong>.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2: Express $\cos \phi$ in terms of $R$ and $Z$</prep-h3>
<prep-p>For a series $RLC$ circuit:</prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Impedance magnitude: $ Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Phase angle: $\tan \phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Therefore, $\cos \phi = \dfrac{R}{Z}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 3: Compare with answer choices</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Option A. $ \tfrac{Z}{R} $ → reciprocal, not correct.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Option B. $ \tan \phi $ → not correct.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Option C. $ \cot \phi $ → not correct.  </prep-p>
<prep-p>Option D. <prep-strong>$ \tfrac{R}{Z} $</prep-strong> → matches $\cos \phi$. ✅</prep-p>

<prep-h3>✅ Final Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \text{The ratio of true power to apparent power is } \frac{R}{Z}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p><prep-strong>Correct option: D</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>In series LCR circuit R $=18 \Omega$ and impedance is $30 \Omega$. An rms voltage 210 V is applied across the circuit. The true power consumed in AC circuit is nearly</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A radioactive element having half-life 30 min . is undergoing beta decay. The fraction of radioactive element remains undecayed after 90 min . will be</prep-p>

$$  \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{N}_0}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{\frac{t}{T}}  $$

</prep-p>
<prep-p>

Here, 

$ t = 90 $ min (total time passed), and

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The magnetic moment of electron due to orbital motion is proportional to ( $\mathrm{n}=$ principal quantum number)</prep-p>

<prep-p>$ \mu = \frac{e}{2m} L, $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where $L$ is the orbital angular momentum.</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 2. Angular momentum in Bohr model</prep-h3>
<prep-p>From Bohr’s quantization condition:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ L_n = n \hbar. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mu_n = \frac{e}{2m} (n\hbar). $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 3. Relation to Bohr magneton</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \mu_B = \frac{e \hbar}{2m}. $</prep-p>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mu_n = n \mu_B. $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Answer:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>The orbital magnetic moment is <prep-strong>proportional to $n$</prep-strong>.</prep-p>
<prep-p>✅ <prep-strong>Correct option: A. $n$</prep-strong></prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A container contains $4 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{H}_2, 4 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{He}$ and certain amount of 'Ne' at a certain temperature. What is the mass of 'Ne' required so that the partial pressure exerted by 'Ne' is equal to the partial pressure of He ?</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content:
<prep-p>In an ionic solid anions are arranged in hcp array and cations occupy $\frac{2}{3}$ of octahedral voids.</prep-p>
<prep-p>What is the formula of ionic compound? [consider $\mathrm{A}=$ cation; $\mathrm{B}=$ anion]</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-h3>Step 1. Relation between atoms and voids in hcp</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>In <prep-strong>hcp arrangement</prep-strong>, number of anions (B) = $N$.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Number of <prep-strong>octahedral voids</prep-strong> generated = $N$.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Number of <prep-strong>tetrahedral voids</prep-strong> generated = $2N$, but here only octahedral voids matter.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 2. Occupied octahedral voids</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>Cations occupy <prep-strong>2/3 of the octahedral voids</prep-strong>.  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>Hence, number of cations (A) = $\tfrac{2}{3} N$.</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Step 3. Ratio of cations to anions</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ \text{Number of A : Number of B} = \tfrac{2}{3}N : N = 2 : 3 $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Step 4. Formula</prep-h3>
<prep-p>Thus the compound's formula is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \mathrm{A}_2 \mathrm{B}_3 $</prep-p>

<prep-p>✅ Correct Answer: <prep-strong>Option B ($\mathrm{A}_2\mathrm{B}_3$)</prep-strong></prep-p>

<prep-p>$ \Delta T_f = K_f \, m $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$\Delta T_f$ = depression in freezing point  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$K_f$ = cryoscopic constant  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$m$ = molality</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Given:</prep-h3>
<prep-ul>

<prep-li><prep-p>$m = 0.18 \, \text{mol kg}^{-1}$</prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>

<prep-h3>Calculation:</prep-h3>
<prep-p>$ K_f = \frac{\Delta T_f}{m} $</prep-p>

<prep-h3>Final Answer:</prep-h3>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the SI unit of resistivity?</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Resistivity $ \rho $ is related to resistance $ R $ by:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ R = \rho \frac{L}{A} $</prep-p>
<prep-p>where  </prep-p>
<prep-ul>
<prep-li><prep-p>$ R $ has unit ohm ($\Omega$)  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$L$ is length (m)  </prep-p></prep-li>
<prep-li><prep-p>$A$ is cross-sectional area (m$^2$)  </prep-p></prep-li>
</prep-ul>
<prep-p>So,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \rho = R \cdot \frac{A}{L} $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Step 2: Substitute units</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ [\rho] = [\Omega] \cdot \frac{m^2}{m} = \Omega \cdot m $</prep-p>

<prep-p><prep-strong>Final Answer:</prep-strong></prep-p>
<prep-p>$ \text{The SI unit of resistivity is } \Omega \, m $</prep-p>
<prep-p>✅ Option A: $\Omega \, \mathrm{m}$</prep-p>

<prep-p>The electrode (copper) with the higher reduction potential undergoes reduction (cathode) and the electrode (hydrogen) with the lower reduction potential undergoes oxidation (anode)</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ The net cell reaction is:</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \mathrm{H}_{2(\mathrm{~g})}+\mathrm{Cu}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+2} \longrightarrow 2 \mathrm{H}_{(\mathrm{aq})}^{+}+\mathrm{Cu}_{(\mathrm{s})} $$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The vector sum of two forces $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ is perpendicular to their vector difference. Hence forces $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ are</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The sum of the two forces,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \overrightarrow{F_1}=\vec{A}+\vec{B} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(i)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>The difference of the two forces,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \vec{F}_2=\vec{A}-\vec{B} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(ii)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since sum of the two forces is perpendicular to their difference,</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & \vec{F}_1 \cdot \vec{F}_2=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & (\vec{A}+\vec{B}) \cdot(\vec{A}-\vec{B})=0 \\ \Rightarrow \quad & A^2-\vec{A} \cdot \vec{B}+\vec{B} \cdot \vec{A}-B^2=0 \\ \therefore \quad & A^2=B^2 \Rightarrow|A|=|B| \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the forces are equal to each other in magnitude.</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>What is the angle between resultant of $A+B$ and $\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}$.</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>The vector $(A+B)$ will be in plane containing vector $A$ and vector $B$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Vector $(\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B})$ will be perpendicular to the plane containing vector $A$ and $B$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Thus, the angle between $(A+B)$ and $(A \times B)$ is $90^{\circ}$ or $\frac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{rad}$.</prep-p>
<prep-p>Alternate solution</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
&(A+B) \cdot(A \times B)=|A+B||A \times B| \cos \alpha \\
& A \cdot(A \times B)+B \cdot(A \times B)=|A+B||A \times B| \cos \alpha \\
& 0+0=|A+B||A \times B| \cos \alpha \\
& \Rightarrow \quad \cos \alpha=0 \\
& \alpha=90^{\circ} \text { or } \frac{\pi}{2} \mathrm{rad}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>The maximum value of the function $a \sin x+b \cos x$ is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let $\mathrm{f}(x)=\mathrm{a} \sin x+\mathrm{b} \cos x$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Let $\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{r} \cos \theta$ and $\mathrm{b}=\mathrm{r} \sin \theta$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} \therefore \quad \mathrm{f}(x) & =\mathrm{r} \cos \theta \sin x+\mathrm{r} \sin \theta \cos x \\ & =\mathrm{r} \sin (x+\theta) \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & -1 \leq \sin (x+\theta) \leq 1 \\ \Rightarrow & -\mathrm{r} \leq \sin (x+\theta) \leq \mathrm{r} \\ \Rightarrow & -\sqrt{\mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{b}^2} \leq \mathrm{f}(x) \leq \sqrt{\mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{b}^2} \end{aligned}\\ &\therefore \quad \text { The maximum value of } \mathrm{f}(x) \text { is } \sqrt{\mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{b}^2} \text {. } \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>If $A+B=\frac{\pi}{2}$ then the maximum value of $\cos \mathrm{A} \cdot \cos \mathrm{B}$ is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let $y=\cos A \cos B$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & =\cos \mathrm{A} \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\mathrm{A}\right) \quad \ldots\left[\because \mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}=\frac{\pi}{2}\right] \\ & =\cos \mathrm{A} \sin \mathrm{~A} \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \cdot \sin \mathrm{~A} \cos \mathrm{~A} \\ & =\frac{1}{2} \sin 2 \mathrm{~A} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Since $-1 \leq \sin x \leq 1$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$\therefore \quad$ Maximum value of $y$ is $\frac{1}{2}$.</prep-p>
pyqs.sub_topics: Trigonometric Functions of Sum and Difference of Angles

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>$$\mathrm{a}$$ and $$\mathrm{b}$$ are the intercepts made by a line on the co-ordinate axes. If $$3 \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{b}$$ and the line passes through $$(1,3)$$, then the equation of the line is</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let the equation of the line be</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\frac{x}{\mathrm{a}}+\frac{y}{\mathrm{~b}}=1$$ .... (i)</prep-p>
<prep-p>This line passes through the point $$(1,3)$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad & \frac{1}{a}+\frac{3}{b}=1 \\
& \Rightarrow b+3 a=a b \\
& \Rightarrow 2 b=a b \quad ...[\because 3a=b]\\
& \Rightarrow a=2 \\
\therefore \quad & b=3 a=6
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>
<prep-p>Equation (i) becomes,</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>A family consisting of a mother, father and their 8 children ( 4 boys and 4 girls) are to be seated at a round table in a party. How many ways can this be done if the mother and father sit together and the males and females alternate?</prep-p>

pyqs.explanation_content: <prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} & {[x]^2-5[x]+6=0} \\ & \Rightarrow[x]^2-3[x]-2[x]+6=0 \\ & \Rightarrow([x]-3)([x]-2)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow[x]=3 \quad \text { or } \quad[x]=2 \\ & \Rightarrow x \in[3,4) \quad \text { or } \quad x \in[2,3) \\ & \Rightarrow x \in[2,4) \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>If $[x]^2-5[x]+6=0$, where $[\cdot]$ denotes the greatest integer function, then</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
&\text { Given: }\\
&\begin{aligned}
& {[x]^2-5[x]+6=0} \\
& \text { Let }[x]=\mathrm{a} \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}^2-5 \mathrm{a}+6=0 \\
& \Rightarrow(\mathrm{a}-2)(\mathrm{a}-3)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=2 \text { or } \mathrm{a}=3 \\
& \Rightarrow[x]=2 \text { or }[x]=3 \\
& \Rightarrow x \in[2,3) \text { or } x \in[3,4) \\
& \Rightarrow x \in[2,4)
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>If $\mathrm{f}(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}\operatorname{m} x+1, & x \leqslant \frac{\pi}{2} \\ \sin x+\mathrm{n}, & x>\frac{\pi}{2}\end{array}\right.$, is continuous at $x=\frac{\pi}{2},(\mathrm{~m}, \mathrm{n} \in \mathbb{Z})$ then</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>If $\mathrm{f}(x)=\log _{x^2}(\log x)$, then at $x=\mathrm{e}, \mathrm{f}^{\prime}(x)$ has the value</prep-p>

pyqs.pyq_content: <prep-p>If $0< x<1$, then $\sqrt{1+x^2}\left[\left\{x \cos \left(\cot ^{-1} x\right)+\sin \left(\cot ^{-1} x\right)\right\}^2-1\right]^{\frac{1}{2}}$ is equal to</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content:
<prep-p>Let $\cot ^{-1} x=\theta$, then $x=\cot \theta$ and</prep-p>
<prep-p>$$\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\pi}{4}< \theta<\frac{\pi}{2} \quad \ldots[\because 0< x<1 \Rightarrow 0<\cot \theta<1] \\
& \therefore \quad \sqrt{1+x^2}\left[\left\{x \cos \left(\cot ^{-1} x\right)+\sin \left(\cot ^{-1} x\right)\right\}^2-1\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
&=\sqrt{1+x^2}\left[\{\cot \theta \cos \theta+\sin \theta\}^2-1\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
&=\sqrt{1+x^2}\left\{\left(\frac{\cos ^2 \theta+\sin ^2 \theta}{\sin \theta}\right)^2-1\right]^{\frac{1}{2}} \\
&=\sqrt{1+x^2} \sqrt{\operatorname{cosec}^2 \theta-1} \\
&=\sqrt{1+x^2}|\cot \theta| \\
&=\left(\sqrt{1+x^2}\right)|x| \\
&=x \sqrt{1+x^2} \\
& \ldots[\because 0< x<1]
\end{aligned}$$</prep-p>

pyqs.d: <prep-p>$\cos x=\mathrm{c} \sin y$, where c is the constant of integration.</prep-p>
pyqs.explanation_content: <prep-p>$$ \begin{aligned} &\begin{aligned} & \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{~d} x}=\cot x \cot y \\ & \Rightarrow \cot x \mathrm{~d} x-\tan y \mathrm{~d} y=0 \end{aligned}\\ &\text { Integrating on both sides, we get }\\ &\begin{aligned} & \log (\sin x)-\log (\sec y)=\log c \\ & \Rightarrow \log \left(\frac{\sin x}{\sec y}\right)=\log c \Rightarrow \sin x=c \sec y \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$</prep-p>
